modules.title: What investing and trading mean
modules.subtitle: Start with goals, time horizons, and uncertainty
modules.objective: Distinguish saving, investing, and trading; calculate a simple return and explain why a profit is uncertain.
modules.content:
## The idea

Saving sets money aside for future use. Investing commits capital to an asset with an uncertain future payoff. Trading buys and sells assets in an attempt to benefit from price changes. Their boundaries overlap: an investor still trades when entering or leaving a position. The useful distinction is the purpose, holding period, and evidence behind the decision.

A long-term investor might study a business's ability to generate cash over years. A short-term trader might study an order imbalance over minutes. Neither time horizon guarantees success. Start by asking: **What am I buying, why might it pay me, when might I need the money, and how could I lose it?**

## A worked example

Maya spends $200 on a fictional investment and later receives $220 when she sells it. Ignoring costs and distributions, the gain is $20 and the return is $20 / $200 = 10%. If the sale brings $170 instead, the return is −15%. A hoped-for 10% return is an expectation, not money already earned.

$$R = \frac{\text{ending value} - \text{starting value}}{\text{starting value}}$$

Always state the time period. A 10% return over one month and a 10% return over five years are different outcomes. Compare investments over matching periods and account for costs before deciding which performed better.

## Build a decision before a position

Write a goal, a time horizon, a reason for the investment, and a condition that would invalidate that reason. Money needed soon has less time to recover from a fall. A promise of high returns with no risk is a reason to investigate the claim, not a substitute for evidence.

For this course, use hypothetical money. No brokerage account or coding experience is needed. Reading, arithmetic, and explaining your choices are enough. The optional Python example lets you change the numbers; its separate synthetic trading rule is not a recommended strategy.

## Connect to later courses

Graham & Dodd develops the distinction between price and estimated value. Statistical foundations teaches how to express uncertainty instead of treating a successful outcome as proof of skill.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Stocks, shares, and business ownership
modules.subtitle: Understand what a stockholder actually owns
modules.objective: Explain equity ownership, market capitalization, dividends, and why share price alone does not measure value.
modules.content:
## The idea

A share of stock is an ownership interest in a company. Common equity is a residual claim: creditors and other senior claims come first. Owners can benefit from price appreciation and dividends, but dividends are not automatic and shareholders can lose their investment. Voting rights depend on the share class.

Separate three quantities: **share price** is the market price of one share; **shares outstanding** is the number issued and held; **market capitalization** is their product. Market capitalization describes the market value of equity, not the company's cash balance or an independent estimate of what the business is worth.

## A worked example

Fictional Harbor Foods has 1,000,000 shares outstanding at $20 each. Its equity market capitalization is $20 million. Owning 100 shares means owning 100 / 1,000,000 = 0.01% of that share class, worth $2,000 at the quote. A declared $0.50 dividend per share would pay $50 on those 100 shares before taxes.

$$\text{Market capitalization} = \text{price per share}\times\text{shares outstanding}$$

Another company has 100 million shares trading at $2, so its market capitalization is $200 million. Its lower share price does not make the entire business cheaper than Harbor Foods.

## Splits and dilution

In a two-for-one stock split, 100 shares become 200; a theoretical $20 price becomes $10. The split itself leaves the $2,000 position value and ownership fraction unchanged. Real market prices may also move that day. A new share issuance is different: if your share count stays fixed while total shares increase, your ownership percentage falls. The company may receive new capital in exchange.

A dividend is a distribution of company resources, not free additional wealth. All else equal, distributing cash reduces the company's value. Later return calculations include both price changes and cash distributions.

## Connect to later courses

Security analysis uses diluted shares and the priority of claims to calculate per-share value. Keep the denominator and the company-wide amounts consistent.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: How stock markets work
modules.subtitle: Meet issuers, investors, brokers, exchanges, and indexes
modules.objective: Trace a stock transaction and distinguish the primary market, secondary market, an index, and an ETF.
modules.content:
## The idea

In a primary-market offering, a company issues new securities to raise money. In the secondary market, existing securities change hands between investors. When you buy already-issued shares from another investor, your payment generally goes to that seller, not to the company.

A broker receives and routes your order. An exchange or other trading venue brings together buying and selling interest. Market makers quote prices at which they are willing to trade, subject to available size. Clearing and settlement handle the obligations after execution. A submitted order, a filled trade, and completed settlement are different stages.

Hours, settlement schedules, lot sizes, currencies, and account rules vary by market and broker. A lesson using dollar amounts does not imply those conventions apply to every exchange.

## A worked example

Harbor Foods issues 100,000 new shares at $20, raising $2 million before offering costs. Later, Maya buys 50 existing shares from Leo for $21 each through a broker. The $1,050 secondary-market payment goes to the selling side; Harbor Foods does not receive another $1,050 in capital from that trade.

## Indexes, funds, and asset classes

An index is a rules-based measure of a basket of assets. An ETF is a fund whose shares trade on a market; it may seek to track an index, pursue an active strategy, or hold a narrow exposure. You buy fund shares, not the abstract index number. Fees and tracking differences can separate fund returns from index returns.

| Instrument | Basic economic claim | A question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stock | Business ownership | Can the business create durable value? |
| Bond | A debt claim with contractual terms | Can the issuer meet its obligations? |
| Fund / ETF | An interest in a pooled portfolio | What does it hold, and what does it cost? |
| Derivative | A contract tied to an underlying variable | What payoff and obligations does the contract create? |

Owning several funds does not necessarily create different exposures: their largest holdings may overlap. Likewise, an index moving up does not mean every constituent rose.

## Connect to later courses

Factor models use benchmarks; portfolio courses examine the exposures inside funds; execution courses distinguish an order's intent from what actually fills.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Prices, quotes, and order types
modules.subtitle: Read a quote and understand the trade-off between price and execution
modules.objective: Calculate a spread, interpret OHLCV, and choose between market, limit, stop, and stop-limit orders in a hypothetical scenario.
modules.content:
## The idea

The **bid** is a quoted buying price and the **ask** a quoted selling price. Their difference is the spread. The last traded price is a past transaction, so it is not a promise of your next fill. Available quantity matters: a large order can consume several price levels.

OHLCV records the open, high, low, close, and traded volume for a period. A candle summarizes that period; it does not reveal the sequence of every trade. Volume is shares traded, not the number of distinct people buying.

## A worked example

A fictional quote shows bid $49.90 for 100 shares and ask $50.10 for 80 shares. The spread is $0.20. A small market buy may execute near $50.10; a market sell may execute near $49.90. An immediate buy and sell of 10 shares at those prices loses $2 before fees, even if the quotes do not change. A request for 200 shares cannot assume all 200 are available at the displayed ask.

$$\text{Spread}=\text{ask}-\text{bid}$$

## Translate an intention into an order

| Order | Instruction | Main trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market | Trade at available prices | Execution price is uncertain |
| Buy limit | Buy at the limit or lower | May fill partly or not at all |
| Sell limit | Sell at the limit or higher | May fill partly or not at all |
| Stop | Activate a market order when triggered | A gap can produce a worse fill than the stop |
| Stop-limit | Activate a limit order when triggered | The limit can prevent an exit |

For a buy limit of $50 with the best ask at $50.10, the instruction does not permit a $50.10 fill. If the market falls to $50, a fill still depends on available quantity and priority. Trigger conventions differ by venue and broker.

## Connect to later courses

The paper-trading lab demonstrates some order mechanics using hypothetical accounts. Strategy backtests use next-open fills and configurable costs. Neither a candle touching a price nor a stop instruction guarantees a fill at that price.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-14). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Returns, compounding, and trading costs
modules.subtitle: Measure what you keep, over the time you hold
modules.objective: Calculate profit after fees, total return with dividends, and compounded returns; distinguish realized from unrealized gains.
modules.content:
## The idea

Profit in money and return in percent answer different questions. Include the purchase cost, sale proceeds, distributions, and fees. An unrealized gain is a change in the marked value of an open position. A realized gain results from closing it. Both affect your economic wealth, and an unrealized gain can disappear before a sale.

## A worked example

Buy 10 shares at $100 and pay a $2 entry fee: the cash outlay is $1,002. Receive $10 of dividends in total. Sell all 10 shares at $110 and pay a $2 exit fee: sale proceeds are $1,098. The net gain is $1,098 + $10 − $1,002 = $106. The return on the initial cash outlay is $106 / $1,002, approximately 10.58%, before taxes.

$$R_{\text{net}}=\frac{\text{net sale proceeds}+\text{distributions}-\text{initial outlay}}{\text{initial outlay}}$$

Zero commission does not mean zero trading cost. Spreads, slippage, fund expenses, financing, and applicable taxes can affect the outcome. Avoid double counting a spread already embedded in the actual fill prices.

## Returns multiply through time

A $100 position gains 10%, reaching $110, then loses 10%, reaching $99. The combined return is −1%, although the arithmetic average of the two period returns is zero.

$$R_{\text{combined}}=(1+r_1)(1+r_2)-1$$

A decline from $100 to $80 is a 20% loss. Recovering from $80 to $100 requires a 25% gain because the new denominator is smaller. A basis point is 0.01 percentage points: 10 basis points equals 0.10%, or 0.001 as a decimal multiplier. A 10 bp fee on $1,000 is $1.

## Connect to later courses

Statistical foundations develops discounting and annualization. Backtests later separate the strategy return from the benchmark and charge costs at execution. Keep the time period, units, and cash-flow assumptions visible in every comparison.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Reading a business before buying its stock
modules.subtitle: Connect financial statements, earnings, cash, and valuation
modules.objective: Identify the three main financial statements, calculate EPS and P/E, and distinguish a low price from evidence of value.
modules.content:
## The idea

The income statement describes revenues, expenses, and profit over a period. The balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity at a date. The cash-flow statement explains movements in cash from operating, investing, and financing activities. Profit and cash flow differ because recognition and payment need not happen together.

A sale on credit can increase revenue and receivables before cash arrives. Borrowing increases cash and debt without creating sales profit. Buying equipment uses cash immediately, while its accounting expense can be spread over years. Ask what caused each change before declaring the business stronger.

## A worked example

Fictional Cedar Tools reports $12 million revenue, $2 million net income available to common shareholders, and 1 million weighted-average diluted shares. Earnings per share (EPS) is $2. At a $30 share price, the price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) is 15. Its balance sheet shows $15 million assets and $9 million liabilities, leaving $6 million book equity.

$$\mathrm{EPS}=\frac{\text{net income available to common}}{\text{weighted-average diluted shares}},\qquad P/E=\frac{P}{\mathrm{EPS}}$$

Suppose operating cash flow is only $0.4 million because customers have not yet paid. That does not prove fraud, but it raises a useful question about collections and working capital. A second company with a P/E of 8 may be cheaper relative to reported earnings, or those earnings may be about to decline. The multiple alone cannot decide.

## Price, value, and available evidence

Price is a current quote. Value is an estimate based on future cash flows, assets, and risk. Book equity is an accounting residual, not a guaranteed sale value. Compare several periods, examine debt and one-time items, and read the company's published reports.

When simulating a past decision, use only information available at that time. A December reporting period does not make a report released in March available in December. Treat a promotional post as a lead to verify, not as a financial statement.

## Connect to later courses

These distinctions prepare you for normalized earnings, net-current-asset value, senior claims, and margin of safety in Track 01.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks/evaluating-stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Risk, diversification, and position sizing
modules.subtitle: Understand what can go wrong before choosing a quantity
modules.objective: Distinguish company and market risk; calculate a hypothetical position size and explain why stops do not cap every loss.
modules.content:
## The idea

Company risk comes from a particular issuer, such as a failed product. Market risk can affect many investments together, such as a broad repricing of discount rates. Diversification spreads exposure, but correlated holdings can decline at the same time. Ten companies in one narrow industry may share much of the same risk.

Volatility describes variability in returns. Drawdown measures the decline from a previous portfolio peak. Neither alone captures every risk: an illiquid asset can have infrequent price changes and still be hard to sell. Consider liquidity, debt, concentration, and the ability to tolerate losses.

## A worked example

In a paper account with $10,000, a hypothetical plan allocates $100 to the loss between a $50 entry and a $48 exit trigger. Planned risk per share is $2. Dividing $100 by $2 gives 50 shares, a $2,500 position. The $100 budget is 1% of this example account; it is an illustration, not a universal sizing recommendation.

$$q=\left\lfloor\frac{\text{planned risk budget}}{\text{entry price}-\text{planned exit price}}\right\rfloor$$

If a gap leads to an actual $45 exit, the loss is $250 before costs, not $100. Fees and slippage also change the result. The calculation describes a planned scenario, not a maximum loss guarantee. Check the cash required as well as the planned risk; a cash account must be able to fund the purchase.

## Borrowing and short selling

Margin uses borrowed money to increase exposure. If $1,000 of your money and $1,000 of borrowing buy $2,000 of stock, a 10% stock loss removes $200, or 20% of your initial equity, before financing costs. The debt still needs to be repaid. Short selling sells borrowed shares and requires buying them back; rising prices can create losses beyond the initial proceeds. Detailed rules vary by account and market.

## Connect to later courses

Portfolio construction measures co-movement. Risk management studies drawdowns and tail losses. Bot engineering turns exposure limits and stale-price checks into explicit controls.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/getting-started/asset-allocation). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

modules.title: Build your first research and trading plan
modules.subtitle: Bring the fundamentals together and prepare for the advanced tracks
modules.objective: Write a testable paper-trading plan with an entry reason, order, sizing assumptions, exit conditions, costs, and review process.
modules.content:
## The idea

A plan makes a decision reviewable. Write it before observing the outcome. Specify the asset and source, the reason to enter, the evidence that would invalidate the reason, the intended holding period, the order instruction, the quantity, and the expected costs. Record actual fills separately from your intention.

Avoid evaluating a plan only by whether the last trade made money. A disciplined decision can lose; a poorly supported decision can profit by chance. Keep the record of losing trials as well as winners. Compare a strategy against a relevant benchmark over the same period using the same cost conventions.

## A worked example

In a fictional $5,000 paper account, Ari studies Harbor Foods after a published report. The hypothesis is that collections will recover; the invalidating evidence is another deterioration in receivables and operating cash flow. Ari considers 10 shares using a $20 buy limit, reserving roughly $200 plus costs. If the ask stays above $20, the order can remain unfilled.

The plan records an illustrative $18 exit trigger, a $20 planned price loss for 10 shares, and a gap scenario: an actual $15 exit would lose $50 before costs. Ari schedules a review after the next public report. There is no guarantee that the thesis works, the order fills, or the exit matches the trigger.

## Your research note

Use **Add a note** to record your own fictional plan:

1. Asset, source, and information availability date.
2. Hypothesis, holding period, and evidence against it.
3. Entry instruction, quantity, cash required, and cost assumptions.
4. Planned exit, a worse-fill scenario, and concentration check.
5. Benchmark, review date, and the result you will record even if it fails.

Confirmation bias means favoring supporting evidence and overlooking contradictions. Chasing a recent gain without checking the thesis is another common error. Add an explicit reason to wait when the evidence or data is insufficient.

## Choose what to study next

| What you want to understand | Continue with |
| --- | --- |
| Business value and a margin of safety | [Classical value investing](/curriculum/security-analysis) |
| Returns, probability, and evidence | [Statistical foundations](/curriculum/statistical-foundations) |
| Exposures and portfolio risk | [Econometrics & factor models](/curriculum/econometrics) after statistics |
| Testing repeatable rules | [Systematic strategies](/curriculum/strategy-lab) after valuation and statistics |
| Reliable automated execution | [Autonomous stock bots](/curriculum/stock-bots) after strategy testing |
| Tokens and liquidity pools | [Web3 & cryptoeconomics](/curriculum/web3) after risk fundamentals |

Complete the practice questions and final exam to check your readiness. You may revisit any lesson or retake an exam; later tracks remain available for learners who already know the basics.

modules.title: Foundations of Graham & Dodd
modules.subtitle: Investment, speculation, and the margin of safety
modules.content:
## The idea

An investment thesis begins with a claim about value and the evidence that could disprove it. Price is observable; intrinsic value is an estimate. Treat that estimate as a range built from conservative assumptions about assets, earnings, and the claims senior to common equity.

$$
\text{Margin of safety} = 1 - \frac{P}{V}
$$

## A worked example

A company trades at $60. Your conservative, base, and optimistic estimates are $75, $100, and $125. Against the base estimate, the discount is 40%. Against the conservative estimate, it is only 20%. A 30% required margin would reject this purchase under the conservative case.

## Research protocol

Distinguish a quoted discount from a loss guarantee. Financial leverage, a deteriorating business, and a mistaken estimate can consume the entire cushion. Write down a disconfirming observation before considering a purchase.

### In the sandbox

Run the lesson template, then change one assumption at a time. Record the parameter, the observed change, and whether the result supports your original claim. All default price paths are synthetic, and the accompanying trend strategy demonstrates execution mechanics. Its returns do not validate the lesson’s valuation thesis.

exercise.question: At a price of $60 and intrinsic value of $100, what is the margin of safety?
exercise.explanation: Subtract price divided by value from one: 1 − 60/100 = 40%.

intrinsic_value = 100
margin = 1 - price / intrinsic_value
print("Margin of safety:", round(margin * 100, 2), "%")

modules.title: Fixed-income & senior securities
modules.subtitle: Coverage, priority, and the asset cushion
modules.content:
## The idea

A bond is a contractual claim, but the issuer must generate the cash to honor it. Examine payment priority, recurring earnings, and fixed charges across a full cycle. The common shareholder receives what remains after creditors and preferred holders are paid.

$$
\text{Interest coverage} = \frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Interest expense}}
$$

## A worked example

An issuer reports EBIT of $120 million and annual interest expense of $30 million: coverage is 4×. In a recession, EBIT falls to $45 million and coverage becomes 1.5×. If leases add $15 million of fixed charges, an appropriately adjusted numerator and denominator are needed; interest coverage alone is incomplete.

## Research protocol

Reconcile accounting earnings to operating cash flow. Compare the weak-year coverage with covenants, refinancing dates, and liquid assets. Do not infer safety from a single strong year.

Run the lesson template, then change one assumption at a time. Record the parameter, the observed change, and whether the result supports your original claim. modules.title: Normalized earning power
modules.subtitle: Separate recurring performance from accounting noise
modules.content:
## The idea

Reported earnings combine durable operations, cyclical effects, and items unlikely to recur. Build an explicit bridge from reported profit to adjusted profit. Normalization should remove symmetrical gains and losses, rather than merely adding back inconvenient expenses.

$$
\overline{\mathrm{EPS}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathrm{EPS}^{\mathrm{adjusted}}_t
$$

## A worked example

Adjusted earnings per share over five years are $2, $3, $4, $3, and $3. Their arithmetic mean is $3. A one-time property gain of $2 per share in the most recent year would raise reported EPS to $5, but does not raise this normalized estimate.

## Research protocol

Check share-count changes, inflation, and changes in the business mix before averaging. Review inventory methods, provisions, stock compensation, and repeated restructuring costs. A frequently recurring “one-off” is an operating cost.

### In the sandbox

All default price paths are synthetic, and the accompanying trend strategy demonstrates execution mechanics. Its returns do not validate the lesson’s valuation thesis.

modules.title: Balance sheet & asset-based valuation
modules.subtitle: Net-current-asset value and the liquidation test
modules.content:
## The idea

Net-current-asset value gives no credit to fixed assets and deducts all liabilities and preferred claims. It is a deliberately demanding starting point. A separate liquidation analysis applies realistic recovery assumptions to receivables and inventory, recognizing collection costs and deteriorating stock.

$$
\mathrm{NCAV/share} = \frac{\mathrm{Current\ assets}-\mathrm{Total\ liabilities}-\mathrm{Preferred}}{\mathrm{Diluted\ shares}}
$$

## A worked example

Cash of $40 million, receivables of $60 million, and inventory of $80 million sum to $180 million in current assets. With $70 million of liabilities and 10 million shares, NCAV is $11 per share. A two-thirds screen requires a price below $7.33. Haircuts of 15% to receivables and 40% to inventory lower adjusted value to $6.90 per share.

## Research protocol

Use actual filing availability dates. Deduct debt and other liabilities, including obligations that may not appear in current liabilities. Test whether cash burn can exhaust the cushion before value is realized.

modules.title: The Graham valuation formula
modules.subtitle: A sensitivity tool, with explicit limitations
modules.content:
## The idea

The Graham heuristic links earnings and an assumed growth rate. It is useful for seeing how an estimate responds to assumptions; it is not a universal pricing law. Small changes to growth and bond yields can produce large swings in implied value, especially for cyclical firms.

$$
V = \frac{\mathrm{EPS}\,(8.5+2g)\,4.4}{Y}
$$

## A worked example

With EPS of $4, growth g = 5 (five percentage points), and bond yield Y = 4.4 (also in percent), the formula gives $74. Raising Y to 6 reduces the estimate to about $54.27. Entering g = 0.05 would use the wrong units in this historical heuristic.

## Research protocol

Cap growth assumptions and compare with an independently derived DCF and asset valuation. Expensing versus capitalizing research and development changes earnings and reinvestment requirements; keep those adjustments consistent.

### In the sandbox

Run the lesson template, then change one assumption at a time. Record the parameter, the observed change, and whether the result supports your original claim. All default price paths are synthetic, and the accompanying trend strategy demonstrates execution mechanics. Its returns do not validate the lesson’s valuation thesis.

modules.title: Time value of money
modules.subtitle: Discounting cash flows and terminal value
modules.content:
## The idea

Money available today can be invested. To compare future cash flows, discount each at a rate consistent with its timing, currency, and risk. Keep nominal cash flows with nominal rates and real cash flows with real rates.

$$
PV = \sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t}+\frac{CF_{T+1}}{(r-g)(1+r)^T}
$$

## A worked example

A payment of $110 one year from now is worth $100 at a 10% discount rate. For a perpetuity paying $5 next year with growth of 2% and a required return of 7%, value is $100. The growing-perpetuity relation requires r > g.

## Research protocol

Model an explicit forecast period before applying terminal growth. Examine what fraction of value comes from the terminal term and report a discount-rate/growth sensitivity table.

modules.title: Probability distributions in finance
modules.subtitle: Normal, lognormal, and heavy-tailed returns
modules.content:
## The idea

Prices cannot fall below zero in an unlevered cash asset, while returns can be negative. Lognormal price models arise from normal log returns. Real returns often exhibit heavier tails and time-varying volatility than a Gaussian model captures.

$$
\log(S_T/S_0)\sim\mathcal{N}((\mu-\sigma^2/2)T,\sigma^2T)
$$

## A worked example

A one-day normal 99% loss threshold is about 2.33 standard deviations below the mean. If daily volatility doubles from 1% to 2%, the threshold roughly doubles. Heavy tails can still make realized losses beyond this threshold more frequent than the model predicts.

## Research protocol

Generate both GBM and jump-diffusion paths with the same seed. Compare downside quantiles, not just means. A model is an approximation whose assumptions need direct checks.

### In the sandbox

Run the lesson template, then change one assumption at a time. Record the parameter, the observed change, and whether the result supports your original claim. modules.title: Sampling & confidence intervals
modules.subtitle: Estimate uncertainty, not just a point estimate
modules.content:
## The idea

A sample mean varies across samples. Its standard error reflects sample size and dispersion. Serial dependence reduces the effective information in a time series, so the independent-observation formula can be too optimistic.

$$
\overline{x}\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}
$$

## A worked example

If 25 independent observations have a sample mean of 1% and a standard deviation of 5%, the standard error is 1%. A 95% interval uses about 2.064 standard errors, giving approximately −1.064% to 3.064%. The data do not establish a positive mean at this confidence level.

## Research protocol

For dependent returns, use a block bootstrap or a dependence-aware standard error. Record the resampling seed. A confidence interval describes repeated-sampling coverage, not a probability statement about a fixed parameter.

modules.title: Hypothesis testing in markets
modules.subtitle: Distinguish evidence from a lucky backtest
modules.content:
## The idea

State a null hypothesis before looking at the outcome. A p-value measures how incompatible an observation is with the null model; it is not the probability the null is true. Multiple strategy trials demand stronger evidence than a single pre-specified test.

$$
t=\frac{\overline{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}
$$

## A worked example

A test with a 5% significance threshold rejects true nulls about 5% of the time under its assumptions. If you independently test 20 null strategies, the probability of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95²⁰, about 64%.

## Research protocol

Separate model development and final evaluation chronologically. Keep a research log of failed trials and apply family-wise or false-discovery controls appropriate to the research question.

modules.title: Linear regression & correlation
modules.subtitle: Estimate alpha, beta, and explained variation
modules.content:
## The idea

Regress asset excess returns on benchmark excess returns to estimate market exposure and an intercept. The slope describes association conditional on the model. Neither a significant coefficient nor a high R² establishes causation.

$$
r_i-r_f=\alpha+\beta(r_m-r_f)+\epsilon_i
$$

## A worked example

An estimated daily alpha of 0.02% with a standard error of 0.03% has a t-statistic near 0.67. A positive estimate alone is weak evidence of persistent skill. A beta of 1.2 means a one-percentage-point benchmark move is associated with about a 1.2-point asset move in the fitted model.

## Research protocol

Align return timestamps and subtract the same-period risk-free return. Inspect residuals for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation, and use appropriate uncertainty estimates.

modules.title: Multiple regression & diagnostics
modules.subtitle: Partial effects and fragile coefficients
modules.content:
## The idea

A multiple regression attributes returns to several explanatory variables at once. A coefficient is a partial association holding the included regressors constant. Correlated features can make estimates unstable even when predictions appear accurate.

$$
\widehat{\beta}=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y,\qquad \mathrm{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}
$$

## A worked example

If one factor is explained by the remaining factors with R² = 0.90, its VIF is 10. The inflated variance makes its separate contribution hard to identify. Use a numerically stable least-squares decomposition rather than explicitly inverting XᵀX.

## Research protocol

Inspect condition numbers and VIF, test residual variance and dependence, and document whether robust or HAC standard errors are used. Excluding a correlated feature changes the estimand.

modules.title: Time series & cointegration
modules.subtitle: Stationarity, mean reversion, and volatility
modules.content:
## The idea

A stationary process has stable distributional properties over time. Two non-stationary price series may share a stationary linear combination; this is cointegration. Correlated returns alone are insufficient evidence for a mean-reverting price spread.

$$
x_t=c+\phi x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t,\qquad |\phi|<1
$$

## A worked example

For an AR(1) with φ = 0.8, shocks decay geometrically. Its half-life is ln(0.5)/ln(0.8), approximately 3.1 periods. If φ = 1, the process is a random walk and the stationary mean-reversion interpretation fails.

## Research protocol

Estimate hedge ratios using training data only and apply the correct residual-based cointegration test. Stress-test structural breaks. GARCH models conditional variance, not a guarantee of directional predictability.

modules.title: Portfolio theory & factor pricing
modules.subtitle: Diversification depends on covariance
modules.content:
## The idea

Portfolio variance depends on both individual risks and their co-movement. Estimated means are noisy, and unconstrained optimization can produce extreme weights. Shrinkage and position bounds trade theoretical fit for more stable allocations.

$$
\sigma_p^2=w^\top\Sigma w,\qquad \sum_iw_i=1
$$

## A worked example

Two equally weighted assets each have 20% volatility. With zero correlation, portfolio volatility is about 14.14%. With correlation of one, it remains 20%. Diversification is lost precisely when assets begin moving together.

## Research protocol

Distinguish exposure to market, size, value, profitability, investment, and momentum from unexplained alpha. Align factor definitions and timing, and evaluate a constrained portfolio outside the estimation window.

modules.title: Risk & downside metrics
modules.subtitle: Describe the loss distribution honestly
modules.content:
## The idea

Volatility treats gains and losses symmetrically. Drawdown, downside deviation, VaR, and expected shortfall answer different questions. Use them together and disclose the horizon, confidence level, and sign convention.

$$
\mathrm{DD}_t=\frac{V_t}{\max_{s\le t}V_s}-1
$$

## A worked example

A portfolio rises from 100 to 120 and then falls to 90. The drawdown is −25%, despite being only 10% below its initial value. To recover from a 25% loss, it must gain 33.33%.

## Research protocol

Estimate historical VaR from daily loss quantiles, then compute expected shortfall from losses in the tail. Sparse samples make extreme quantiles unstable. In this workspace, VaR and CVaR are reported as positive loss magnitudes.

modules.title: Backtest traps & research hygiene
modules.subtitle: Control what the experiment is allowed to know
modules.content:
## The idea

A backtest should recreate the information set available at each decision. Revised financial statements, surviving-only universes, and same-bar execution all inflate apparent performance. The research process itself can overfit through repeated trials.

$$
\mathrm{Position}_t=f(\mathcal{I}_{t-1})
$$

## A worked example

A filing describing the March quarter becomes public in May. A portfolio formed in April cannot use it. Similarly, a close-derived signal cannot earn the full return of the bar on which that close was observed.

## Research protocol

Archive point-in-time data and use next-open fills. Log strategy versions and split data chronologically. Reserve a final untouched test and disclose delisted-security coverage before interpreting a historical screen.

Build a universe at each rebalance date, select the latest statements actually published, and compute per-share net-current-asset value. A price below two-thirds of NCAV is a candidate screen, not a complete investment decision.

modules.content:
## The idea

Standardize earnings yield, invested-capital returns, and coverage within a contemporaneous universe. A composite score expresses an explicit preference rather than discovering an objective ranking. Avoid scale differences dominating the combination.

$$
\mathrm{Score}_i=\tfrac13[z(E/P)_i+z(ROIC)_i+z(\mathrm{Coverage})_i]
$$

## A worked example

Suppose a company’s standardized scores are 1.2 for earnings yield, 0.6 for ROIC, and −0.3 for coverage. Its equal-weight composite is 0.5. A debt-heavy company may look cheap on P/E while failing the coverage test.

## Research protocol

Winsorize using training-universe thresholds and neutralize sector exposures only if the thesis requires it. Track accounting definitions and compare with a simple equal-weight baseline.

modules.title: Statistical arbitrage pairs
modules.subtitle: Trade a spread with explicit exit conditions
modules.content:
## The idea

A pairs strategy trades deviations in a statistically justified spread. Estimate a hedge ratio and a spread mean and scale from past observations. Entry and exit thresholds must be set before observing the test-period outcome.

$$
z_t=\frac{s_t-\overline{s}_{t-L:t-1}}{\sigma_{s,t-L:t-1}}
$$

## A worked example

A spread of 8 with a trailing mean of 2 and standard deviation of 3 has z = 2. A mean-reversion rule might short the spread, while a risk rule exits if the relationship breaks. Hedging notional value alone does not ensure beta or dollar neutrality.

## Research protocol

Include short borrow, both legs’ commissions, and asynchronous fill risk. Re-estimate with a walk-forward schedule. Never assume that a historically stationary spread cannot undergo a permanent change.

modules.title: Cross-sectional machine learning
modules.subtitle: Predict with a chronological research design
modules.content:
## The idea

Train regularized models on features known at prediction time. Cross-sectional ranking may be more stable than forecasting exact returns. The target horizon determines the embargo and overlap handling required between train and test sets.

$$
\widehat{\beta}=\arg\min_\beta\left\{\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2\right\}
$$

## A worked example

A 20-day forward return label for a training observation on January 31 contains February prices. A test fold beginning February 1 overlaps that information. Purge overlapping labels and apply an embargo appropriate to the design.

## Research protocol

Fit scaling and feature selection on training data only. Compare ridge and tree models with simple factor ranks. Report net turnover-adjusted outcomes and every material hyperparameter search.

modules.title: Event-driven bot architecture
modules.subtitle: Separate signals from execution and state
modules.content:
## The idea

A reliable bot separates market ingestion, signal generation, sizing, order routing, and the audit trail. Each event has an identity and a timestamp. Replaying an event must not create a second unintended order.

$$
\mathrm{Event}\rightarrow\mathrm{Signal}\rightarrow\mathrm{Risk}\rightarrow\mathrm{Order}\rightarrow\mathrm{Fill}
$$

## A worked example

A process crashes after the broker accepts an order but before local confirmation. On restart, blindly retrying may double the position. Store an idempotent client order ID and reconcile broker state before retrying.

## Research protocol

Keep an append-only event log and a durable position snapshot. Treat missing acknowledgments as unknown state. This course uses a local mock broker, with no connection to a live brokerage account.

modules.title: Rule-based strategy bots
modules.subtitle: Build a rebalancer with observable rules
modules.content:
## The idea

A rule-based bot transforms an information event into a target portfolio. Rebalancing computes the difference between current and desired holdings. Signal generation and execution frequency need not be the same.

$$
\Delta q_i=\frac{w_i^{*}V}{P_i}-q_i
$$

## A worked example

A $100,000 portfolio targets a 10% allocation to an asset priced at $50. Its target is 200 shares. If 120 shares are already held, the raw order is 80 shares before commissions, lot sizes, and cash constraints.

## Research protocol

Schedule filing-driven value screens, spread-driven pairs rules, or trend rules independently. Test stale data and reject oversized orders. Log the inputs that produced each target.

modules.subtitle: Keep model suggestions inside deterministic limits
modules.content:
## The idea

A predictive model ranks opportunities; a qualitative model can summarize source text and identify risks. Neither should bypass position limits, data provenance checks, or the order approval policy. Treat model output as untrusted structured input.

$$
\mathrm{AllowedOrder}=\mathrm{Signal}\cap\mathrm{DataChecks}\cap\mathrm{RiskLimits}
$$

## A worked example

An LLM identifies an accounting concern in a filing. Save the cited passage, source date, schema version, and confidence rationale. A deterministic rule can veto the candidate, but a fluent summary is not verified financial evidence.

## Research protocol

Evaluate on held-out filings and include adversarial text in tests. Track drift and abstentions. Provider credentials and a separately validated model are required for live inference; the local simulator uses explicit deterministic rules.

modules.title: Position sizing & circuit breakers
modules.subtitle: Design the failure path before the happy path
modules.content:
## The idea

Position sizing couples expected edge to uncertainty and loss tolerance. The Kelly fraction is highly sensitive to estimated probabilities and payoff ratios. Fractional sizing and strict caps reduce exposure to estimation error.

$$
f^*=\frac{pb-(1-p)}{b}
$$

## A worked example

With win probability p = 0.55 and win/loss payoff b = 1, full Kelly is 10%. Half Kelly is 5%. If p is actually 0.48, the strategy has negative expected edge; leverage does not repair a mistaken estimate.

## Research protocol

Set independent drawdown, concentration, stale-data, and spread checks. Persist the halt state and require an explicit reset after investigation. A stop order cannot guarantee its trigger price in a gap.

### In the sandbox

Run the lesson template, then change one assumption at a time. Record the parameter, the observed change, and whether the result supports your original claim. All default price paths are synthetic, and the accompanying trend strategy demonstrates execution mechanics. Its returns do not validate the lesson’s valuation thesis.

exercise.explanation: Full Kelly is 0.10, so half Kelly is 0.05.

payoff = 1
kelly = (probability * payoff - (1 - probability)) / payoff
print("Half Kelly:", round(kelly / 2, 4))

## The idea

Paper trading checks operational behavior using simulated fills. An order acknowledgment is not a fill. Track submitted, partially filled, filled, cancelled, and rejected states, and reconcile cash and holdings after every fill.

\mathrm{Cash}_{t+1}=\mathrm{Cash}_t-qP-\mathrm{Commission}

modules.subtitle: Separate protocol activity from tokenholder value
modules.content:
## The idea

A protocol can be useful without distributing economic value to its token. Examine issuance, unlocks, fee routing, burns, governance rights, and who bears operating costs. Nominal staking yield includes compensation for dilution and risk.

$$
MV=PY
$$

A staking token pays 8% more units while total token supply grows 6%. A simple dilution-adjusted unit yield is 1.08/1.06 − 1, about 1.89%, before price changes, fees, slashing, and taxes. This is not a risk-free return.

## Research protocol

Read the actual economic rights and contract controls. Never treat proof-of-stake yield as literally risk-free: validator, slashing, liquidity, governance, and smart-contract risks remain.

modules.title: AMMs & impermanent loss
modules.subtitle: Derive swap output from the invariant
modules.content:
## The idea

A constant-product pool quotes trades from reserves rather than matching an order book. A large swap moves the marginal price. Trading fees change the effective input, while liquidity providers bear exposure to relative price movements.

$$
\Delta y=\frac{y\,\Delta x(1-f)}{x+\Delta x(1-f)},\qquad IL(k)=\frac{2\sqrt{k}}{1+k}-1
$$

## A worked example

A pool contains 10 ETH and 20,000 USDC. Selling 1 ETH with no fee returns 20,000/11, about 1,818.18 USDC. The average execution price is worse than the initial 2,000 USDC marginal price. If the external price doubles, full-range impermanent loss is about 5.72% relative to holding.

## Research protocol

Use the AMM simulator to vary trade size, fees, and relative price. Full-range IL omits fee income. Concentrated positions need separate piecewise inventory accounting inside and outside their price ranges.

modules.title: Crypto arbitrage & market neutrality
modules.subtitle: A hedged position still has several kinds of risk
modules.content:
## The idea

Cash-and-carry pairs a long spot position with a short derivative. Positive funding may compensate the short, but the rate can reverse. Delta neutrality does not eliminate liquidation, basis, collateral, custody, or venue risk.

$$
\mathrm{NetCarry}\approx\mathrm{Funding}-\mathrm{Borrow}-\mathrm{Fees}-\mathrm{BasisChange}
$$

## A worked example

At a constant 0.01% funding rate every eight hours, a simple annualized rate is 0.0001 × 3 × 365 = 10.95%. This assumes unchanged rates, no fees, and no compounding; it is not a forward yield guarantee.

## Research protocol

Stress collateral in a price gap, include liquidation rules, and avoid relying on transfers between venues during a crisis. Study MEV as an execution cost and protection problem; no adversarial trading is executed by this platform.

modules.title: Crypto execution engineering
modules.subtitle: Track nonces, confirmations, and transaction costs
modules.content:
## The idea

On-chain execution is an asynchronous state machine. A submitted transaction can remain pending, be replaced, or be removed by a reorganization. Nonces order an account’s transactions; a nonce manager must coordinate concurrent senders.

$$
\mathrm{EffectiveGasPrice}=\min(\mathrm{MaxFee},\mathrm{BaseFee}+\mathrm{PriorityFee})
$$

## A worked example

With a base fee of 20 gwei, a priority fee of 2 gwei, and a max fee of 30 gwei, the effective price is 22 gwei. If the base fee rises above the cap, the transaction cannot be included on those terms. A higher tip still cannot guarantee inclusion.

## Research protocol

Persist transaction intents before signing, reconcile receipts, and choose a confirmation policy. Keep keys outside lesson code. The local course provides simulation only and never requests a wallet seed phrase.

modules.title: Crypto stress testing
modules.subtitle: Model liquidity loss and collateral shortfalls
modules.content:
## The idea

A stress test asks what happens under an adverse scenario rather than estimating its likelihood. Model a rapid price drop, collateral haircuts, widening spreads, and the inability to rebalance. Correlations and liquidity often deteriorate together.

$$
\mathrm{HealthFactor}=\frac{\mathrm{CollateralValue}\times\mathrm{LiquidationThreshold}}{\mathrm{DebtValue}}
$$

## A worked example

Collateral worth $10,000, a liquidation threshold of 80%, and debt of $5,000 imply a health factor of 1.6. A 50% collateral-price drop lowers it to 0.8, before interest and fees, potentially triggering liquidation.

## Research protocol

Use the flash-crash scenario and evaluate the path to liquidation, not merely the final price. For LP positions compare fee income with inventory loss, gas, and execution slippage.
